Grief & Loss

Grief & Loss: Carrying What Cannot Be Fixed

Grief is not a staircase you climb. It is weather you learn to live inside.

Overview

Oscillation, not stages

Grief is not only about death. It follows divorce, diagnosis, estrangement, miscarriage, and the loss of a future you had assumed. Any of those can produce the full physical weight of mourning.

The five-stage model was originally observed in dying patients, not the bereaved, and was never intended as a checklist. Grief does not progress tidily, and revisiting an earlier feeling is not regression.

Symptom mechanics

Current models describe grief as moving back and forth between confronting the loss and attending to ongoing life. Both are necessary. A morning of laughter does not undo mourning, and a wave of sorrow two years on is not a relapse.

Grief also lives in the body: appetite changes, disrupted sleep, chest heaviness, and a real hit to concentration and immune function. This is why practical care — food, water, sleep — is legitimate grief work.

Signs & symptoms

What it looks like in the body, the mind, and the day

These are patterns, not a diagnosis. Filter by where you notice them most.

  • Mind

    Waves rather than a slope

    Intensity arrives suddenly, often triggered by something small and ordinary.

  • Body

    Physical heaviness

    Chest pressure, aching limbs, and exhaustion that sleep does not touch.

  • Behavior

    Searching behaviour

    Scanning crowds, rereading messages, keeping a phone number active.

  • Mind

    Guilt and rehearsal

    Replaying what might have been said or done differently.

Myths vs facts

What people believe, and what the evidence says

  • Myth

    Grief lasts about a year.

    Fact

    There is no schedule. Acute grief often softens over months, but adaptation continues for years and anniversaries stay tender.

  • Myth

    Staying busy is the healthiest approach.

    Fact

    Distraction has a place, but grief that is never approached tends to surface as physical symptoms or sudden collapse.

  • Myth

    Moving forward means letting go.

    Fact

    Most people keep a continuing bond with the person they lost. Integration, not erasure, is the goal.

Coping strategies

Evidence-based tools you can try today

Each of these is drawn from an established therapy protocol. Start with one and repeat it — a tool used badly twice beats a tool read about once.

  1. 01

    Continuing-bond letters

    Keeps the relationship present in a form you control.

    • Write to them, not about them — present tense.
    • Include ordinary news, not only sorrow.
    • Stop when it becomes heavy; there is no requirement to finish.
  2. 02

    Anniversary planning

    Removes the dread of being ambushed by a date.

    • Mark the date and decide in advance who you want nearby.
    • Choose one small ritual — a walk, a meal they loved, a candle.
    • Give yourself explicit permission to cancel everything else.
  3. 03

    Baseline care card

    Reduces daily decisions to a short, achievable list.

    • Write four items: water, one meal, outside air, one message answered.
    • Keep it visible in the kitchen.
    • Treat a partly ticked card as a completed day.

Treatment pathways

What professional help actually looks like

You do not need to know which of these you want before making an appointment. A clinician's first job is helping you choose.

  • GC

    Grief-focused counselling

    Individual or group support that normalises the process and helps rebuild routine and identity after a loss.

  • CGT

    Complicated Grief Treatment

    A structured therapy for prolonged grief disorder, where intense yearning persists past twelve months and blocks daily function.

  • MD

    Medical review

    Useful when sleep, appetite, or chest symptoms persist, both to treat them and to rule out physical causes.

For the people nearby

How to support a loved one

Say the person’s name. Grieving people are usually more afraid of the loss being forgotten than of being reminded of it. Show up on the ordinary Tuesday, not only at the funeral.

Try saying
  • “I remember when she used to do this — I still think about it.”
  • “I have no words that help, but I am not going anywhere.”
  • “I am coming over Saturday to do the laundry, not to talk.”
Avoid
  • “They are in a better place now.”
  • “Everything happens for a reason.”
  • “At least you had many years together.”

Questions

Frequently asked

If after twelve months there is persistent, intense yearning with an inability to function, prolonged grief disorder may apply and specific treatment helps.

Immediate help · 24/7

If tonight feels unsurvivable, talk to someone now.

These lines are free, confidential, and staffed around the clock. You do not need to be in danger to use them — distress is reason enough.

  • Call or text 988988 Suicide & Crisis LifelineFree, confidential support 24/7 for anyone in emotional distress — not only suicidal crisis.
  • Text HOME to 741741Crisis Text LineText-first support with a trained volunteer crisis counselor, usually within five minutes.
  • Call 1-800-662-4357SAMHSA National HelplineTreatment referrals and information for substance use and co-occurring conditions.
